titulo.texto: The Tilma and the Moving Walkway

frase_gancho.texto: From here you can see the image without stopping.

puente_narrativo.texto: Move forward to the high altar, where the image is found.

guion_corto.texto: In front of you, above the high altar, is the image of Our Lady of Guadalupe, on the tilma that tradition attributes to Juan Diego. It is a cloth made of maguey fiber. So that everyone can see it without stopping, a moving walkway passes beneath it. The image arrived at this Basilica on the twelfth of October, nineteen seventy-six. Before that, it was in the Old Basilica from seventeen oh nine. The Guadalupan tradition tells that the image appeared on the tilma in fifteen thirty-one. The oldest documents that speak of an image of the Virgin venerated at Tepeyac date from fifteen fifty-six.

guion_largo.texto:
In front of you, above the high altar, is the image of Our Lady of Guadalupe. For many people, who come on foot from far away, this is the central point of the visit.

So that thousands of people can see it every day, there is a moving walkway beneath the altar. It advances slowly and carries each visitor for a few moments in front of the image, without anyone having to stop. The Archdiocese has reported that on the feast day of the twelfth of December, more than fifteen thousand people pass along this walkway every hour.

The image is on a tilma, a cloak of maguey fiber cloth. According to the Guadalupan tradition, on the twelfth of December, fifteen thirty-one, Juan Diego presented it to Bishop Fray Juan de Zumárraga. That tradition tells that the image of the Virgin appeared on it. This is how the faithful experience it.

Let us now look at what the documents record. The Tepeyac chapel is mentioned in writing in fifteen fifty-four. In fifteen fifty-six, a file of Archbishop Alonso de Montúfar speaks of devotion to an image of the Virgin. That image was in the chapel. The texts that narrate the apparitions were published in sixteen forty-eight and sixteen forty-nine. Since then, the story has been studied from the perspective of faith and of historical research.

With the passing of the centuries, the devotion grew. Between sixteen twenty-nine and sixteen thirty-four there was a flood. The image was in the Cathedral of Mexico and returned to Tepeyac on the fifteenth of May, sixteen thirty-four. In seventeen thirty-seven, Mexico City swore her as its patroness. In seventeen forty-six, her patronage was extended to all of New Spain. In seventeen fifty-four, Pope Benedict the Fourteenth approved a Mass and a feast of their own for the twelfth of December.

In seventeen fifty-one, the painter Miguel Cabrera examined the image, and years later he published a study about it. On the twelfth of October, eighteen ninety-five, the image received its pontifical coronation in the Old Basilica. Pope Leo the Thirteenth authorized it.

On the twelfth of October, nineteen seventy-six, it was moved to this church. That same year, on the twelfth of December, the first Mañanitas were sung here. Every year, at midnight on that date, many people gather to sing them.

On the thirty-first of July, two thousand two, in this very Basilica, Pope John Paul the Second proclaimed Juan Diego a saint. Earlier, in nineteen ninety, he had declared him blessed.

Many people pass through here in silence, others pray, and others simply observe. All of them share the same space, and each one experiences it in their own way.

texto: Observe the moving walkway beneath the image
Move forward without stopping, as the pilgrims do
